69fb645b54:
This chapter is about matching each kind of question and each kind of data to a retriever. The answer might come from a SQL or API call, a lexical index, a vector index, a fusion of both, a filtered or graph-aware search, or a multi-step agentic search. You'll also see when query rewriting and reranking earn their latency. Then you'll turn all of that into a latency budget and a per-segment accuracy gate you can defend in an ADR.

The simplest configuration that clears every number on the requirements card wins. The examples come from telecom support, network operations and retail. There is Python you can run, and a Java/Spring analogue.
3136115372:
Reading time: 3.5 to 4 hours  ·  Companion code, 18 runnable examples plus a Java file: ccarp-companion/09-retrieval-strategies/ (run bash run_all.sh; every example works offline with --mock).

Corpus, policies, vectors, latencies and prices in the examples are illustrative. The toy vectors and the reranker are stand-ins, not models. Product behaviour that can change (index parameters, hosted reranker options, embedding providers) is marked check the docs. Exam facts for CCAR-P come from third-party summaries of the published blueprint, so verify them against the official exam guide.

Chapter 8 built the indexes this chapter queries. Chapter 11 covers evaluation methodology, and chapter 10 covers production observability.
25eff29303:
Choose the retriever from the shape of the data and the shape of the question, not from fashion: rows go to SQL or an API, exact identifiers go to a lexical index, meaning goes to a vector index, real traffic goes to both fused, and a multi-step search is the last resort.

Then add rewriting, reranking and extra hops one at a time, keep each only if it fixes a measured per-segment failure and still fits the latency budget, and write the numbers down.
5354f25b58:
Everything in this chapter follows from those two sentences.

A retrieval system is a set of components. Each buys a little recall or precision, and each charges a little latency, money and operational risk. A request for "the ERR-5G-4471 runbook" and a request for "how do I get out of my contract early" are different problems that happen to use the same chat box. Send both through one vector index, and it will do well on one and badly on the other. The overall average will hide that.

The exam objective is worded carefully: retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern, and accuracy–latency trade-offs. "Matched" means you read the scenario for its data and its queries before you read the options. "Trade-offs" means every improvement has a price, and you must be able to state it in milliseconds and points of recall.
dd529c7e90:
On the exam, this appears as a scenario with a data source, a query pattern and a constraint, followed by four plausible designs. The constraint might be "p95 under two seconds", "answers must cite the exact order", or "99 percent of error-code lookups must return the right article".

The wrong answers are usually sophisticated. A reranker where SQL was needed. A vector store for order numbers. An agent loop under a tight latency budget. A larger embedding model where the fix was a tokenizer setting. The right answer fits the shape of the data and the budget, and it is the simplest one that does.

A senior engineer's instinct from relational databases transfers directly. You would not run a full-text search to compute a sum, and you would not scan a table for a primary key. The same reasoning applies one layer up.
2200c1978c:
The blueprint for Domain 3 (Integration) lists several objectives. Chapter 6 covers integration mechanisms and capability bloat. Chapter 7 covers authentication and authorisation. Chapter 8 covers the RAG pipeline (chunking and indexing).

This chapter covers retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern and accuracy–latency trade-offs. It assumes you have the chunks, metadata and indexes of chapter 8, and asks what to do at query time.
21f0e6e341:
Search began as a library problem. Early systems matched Boolean expressions over index terms assigned by a human cataloguer. A document had the term or it did not, and the result was an unordered set.

Gerard Salton's SMART system at Cornell in the 1960s treated documents and queries as vectors of weighted terms and ranked by similarity. That gave ranked results instead of sets. In 1972 Karen Spärck Jones published the idea we now call inverse document frequency: a term that appears in few documents tells you more than one that appears in many.

TF-IDF, the product of a term's frequency in a document and its inverse document frequency, became the default weighting for decades. Every lexical engine you will meet descends from it. The intuition survives unchanged in the BM25 formula of section 07: rare words carry the score.
616dd328b1:
Stephen Robertson and colleagues developed a probabilistic framework for ranking at City University London and built the Okapi system. Their BM25 weighting (Robertson and Walker, SIGIR 1994, refined for TREC-3) added two practical corrections to TF-IDF. First, term frequency saturates, so the tenth occurrence of a word adds much less than the second. Second, long documents are penalised, because a long document matches more words by chance.

Lucene-based engines such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch moved their default similarity from TF-IDF to BM25 around 2016 (check the docs for the version in your engine). Earlier, Latent Semantic Indexing (Deerwester et al., 1990) tried to match meaning by decomposing the term–document matrix. It was an early ancestor of embeddings.
ba381db1db:
Word embeddings (word2vec, 2013) put words with similar contexts near each other in a vector space. Sentence and passage encoders followed. In 2020, Karpukhin et al. showed that a dense passage retriever trained on question–passage pairs could beat BM25 on open-domain question answering. Lewis et al. combined a retriever with a generator under the name retrieval-augmented generation. At the same time ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) proposed late interaction, keeping one vector per token.

Approximate nearest-neighbour search made this practical at scale. The HNSW graph index (Malkov and Yashunin, 2016) is now the usual choice in vector databases and in Postgres' pgvector.

The honest summary of the next few years of benchmarks has two parts. Dense retrieval wins on paraphrase and loses on rare exact tokens. And the combination beats either alone on most mixed workloads.
2d4534ed11:
Two ideas from outside the dense wave matter just as much.

Reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009) combined ranked lists by summing 1/(k + rank). It beat sophisticated learning-to-rank methods and needed no score calibration. k = 60 was their constant.

In 2019 Nogueira and Cho used BERT as a cross-encoder to re-rank the top candidates of a BM25 first stage. The model reads the query and the passage together. That is far more accurate than comparing two independently computed vectors, and far too slow to run over a whole corpus.

The two-stage shape is the template for everything in sections 09 to 12: a cheap recall-oriented first stage, then an expensive precision-oriented second stage.
536120e1e3:
Large language models made the query a thing you can transform. HyDE (Gao et al., 2022) generated a hypothetical answer and embedded that instead of the question. Conversational systems learned to rewrite a follow-up into a standalone query. Decomposition split a compound question into sub-questions.

In September 2024 Anthropic described contextual retrieval. You prepend a short, model-written situating context to each chunk before embedding and before building the BM25 index, and combine that with BM25, fusion and reranking. The post reported large reductions in failed retrievals from the combination. Treat those figures as a reason to test the idea on your corpus (chapter 8 part 4), not as a number to quote.

From late 2024 the dominant pattern in practice became agentic retrieval: expose search as a tool and let the model decide what to search next. It handles multi-hop questions that no fixed pipeline anticipated, and it charges for that in calls, latency and variance. The pattern ladder of chapter 2 applies to retrieval exactly as it applies to everything else.
78354ae6e4:
It is tempting to treat retrieval as a single quality dial: better embeddings, higher accuracy. In fact the dial is a collection of separate failure modes with separate cures. A relevant chunk can:

  • fail to be retrieved at all (a recall failure);
  • be retrieved but ranked below the cut-off the generator sees (a ranking failure);
  • be retrieved and then ignored or misread by the model (a use failure);
  • be retrieved correctly but be out of date or forbidden (a correctness or permission failure).

Each of these has a different owner and a different fix, and the architect's first job is to keep them apart. A change that raises recall@50 does nothing for a ranking failure. A better reranker does nothing for a chunk that was never in the candidate set.
249b1a73c7: Every stage you add between the question and the model also has a price in four currencies. Exam scenarios usually hinge on one of them.
9b6723ba1b:
Recall at k is the fraction of the relevant chunks that appear in the top k. Precision at k is the fraction of the top k that is relevant. Early stages exist to maximise recall: do not lose the answer. Late stages exist to maximise precision: put the answer where the model will use it, and keep junk out of the prompt.

Both are measured per query segment, not overall, for the reason the requirements card in section 04 spells out. The segments have different data shapes and different failure causes, and an average lets a strong segment pay for a failing one. Companion example 07 runs four configurations over five segments. No single configuration passes every segment bar, and the best one differs by segment.
9fb9d24f1f:
A user feels the slowest part of a request. And a pipeline of independent stages is slower at the 95th percentile than any stage is on its own. Section 15 builds this carefully. For now, hold three numbers in your head:

  • a vector or lexical search over tens of thousands of chunks typically takes tens of milliseconds;
  • a cross-encoder rerank of fifty candidates takes on the order of a hundred;
  • a model call, whether for rewriting or for an agent step, takes hundreds of milliseconds to seconds.

All of these are planning numbers, so measure yours. That ordering explains how this chapter's architecture is built. Do the cheap, parallelisable work first. Spend the model calls where measurement says they pay. And keep the number of sequential model calls before the first token as low as the requirements allow.
11f509b79d:
Embedding the query is nearly free, and a search is cheap. A hosted reranker charges per document scored or per search (check the docs for the current unit). An LLM-based reranker or rewriter charges per token, like any other model call. A rewrite call on a small model adds a few hundred input tokens and a few dozen output tokens per request.

An agent loop adds that again for every step, plus the growing history. Its cost per request varies by several times between the median and the tail. If you priced the median, that breaks the unit economics of chapter 1. Variance is a cost in its own right: a budget you cannot predict is a budget you cannot cap.
2cba3afa52:
A fixed pipeline has a path you can draw: this query went to the SQL tool, these ten chunks passed the ACL filter, this reranker ordered them. An agentic loop has a trace. Both can be audited. But the cost of proving that no unauthorised chunk reached the prompt rises with the number of places a chunk can enter.

Permissions belong in the retrieval query itself (section 10), not in a post-hoc cleaner. A system with many retrieval paths has many places where that rule can be forgotten.
b24d5c1d9e: Chapter 1 introduced the requirements card: a one-page statement of what the system must do, with numbers. A retrieval-backed assistant needs a few extra lines on the card, and each is a number you will test against. Without them, an architect ends up optimising whatever is easy to measure.
21d95544a4:
The guide-authored contract scenario makes the point. It has a 95 percent floor for each type and a 96 percent overall figure, and a launch that must wait because one type sits at 91 percent. The same rule applies to retrieval segments. Say the card requires recall@5 of 0.95 for error-code lookups. A system with 0.97 overall and 0.70 on error codes has failed the requirement, whatever the average says. You cannot pay for a failing segment with a strong one.

That is why the measurement code in the companion (examples 07 and 16) prints one row per segment, with a pass or fail against that segment's bar. It is also why the pick in example 16 requires every bar to be met inside the latency budget.

When a segment is small (10 queries), the interval around its recall is wide. The Wilson 95 percent interval on 9 of 10 hits runs from about 0.60 to 0.98. State that width in the ADR. It is part of the argument for building a larger labelled set before launch (chapter 11).
9c80476c88:
The card gives an end-to-end figure: first token within 2.5 seconds at p95 for chat. Retrieval does not own all of it.

Authentication and session lookup take a few tens of milliseconds, and context assembly a few more. The generation call's time-to-first-token is the largest fixed block. In the planning numbers of example 14 it is around 0.7 seconds at the median and 1.5 at the tail. (An input guard that runs a small model, chapter 13, would add its own block. The example leaves it out.) Subtract the fixed blocks, and what remains is the retrieval slice.

Percentiles do not add, so you cannot subtract p95s from p95s. Instead you simulate the whole pipeline (section 15) and test the p95 of the total. Still, the subtraction gives a first reading of the slack. Here the fixed blocks add up to about 1.6 seconds of p95. That leaves a retrieval slice of roughly 0.9 seconds of a 2.5 second budget, in which to place a rewrite, a rerank or neither.
64e91889d2:
Start from the data. Five shapes matter, and each has a natural retriever.

  • Records in a system of record (orders, bills, usage, inventory) are addressed by keys and aggregated by queries. They belong behind a SQL or API tool.
  • Identifiers inside text (error codes, SKUs, ticket numbers, alarm names) are rare tokens whose exact spelling matters. They belong to a lexical index or a key lookup.
  • Prose (policies, FAQs, runbooks) is queried in natural language, with vocabulary that rarely matches the document's. That is the dense retriever's home ground.
  • Mixed content is prose that contains codes and names, which is what most real knowledge bases are. It wants both retrievers fused.
  • Linked or versioned content (rules that reference rules, policies that supersede policies, runbooks that point to other runbooks) wants metadata filters. Where the links are explicit and the questions follow them, it also wants a one-hop expansion.
9632264d53:
The router itself is a component with an accuracy figure. Example 01 implements it as a handful of regular expressions and scores it against 24 labelled requests.

In production, a rule router handles the unambiguous cases: a request containing only a code, or a request that names an account and asks for a total. A small model, such as Haiku 4.5 (check the docs for current model names and prices), handles the rest, with its label validated against an allowed set.

The mistake is the one chapter 2 warned about: treating the router as a prompt rather than a component. Give it a labelled set, report its confusion matrix, and decide what each wrong cell costs. A misroute from "account facts" to "documents" produces a plausible, wrong, unaudited number. A misroute from "lexical" to "hybrid" produces a slightly different ranking.
583c1b0bca:
The most common retrieval mistake in a first enterprise RAG system is to index data that is not text.

Take a telecom assistant that must answer "how much data did line 2 use last month". It has a perfectly good source of truth: the usage table in the billing system. But someone serialises the rows into sentences ("account A-100 line 2 month 2025-09 used 4,211 megabytes"), embeds them, and asks the vector index for the nearest neighbours of the question. What comes back is a set of rows that look like the question. They may be from the right account or a different one, from the right month or a nearby one. The model then adds them up, or worse, picks one.

Three separate things are wrong. The retrieved set is not the right set, because similarity is not a WHERE clause. The arithmetic is done by a language model over a handful of rows instead of by the database over all of them. And the data in the index is a snapshot, stale from the moment the next usage record posts.
5afbd0342e:
A better embedding won't fix this. The fix is to recognise that the question has a structure (an account, a line, a period, an aggregate). The system that owns that structure already answers it exactly.

Expose that system to the model as a tool with typed parameters. Then let the model do what it is good at: deciding that this question needs that tool, and phrasing the result. Chapter 2 covers the pattern. Chapter 7 covers the rule that matters most here: the account identifier comes from the verified session, never from the model's text.
ea28f7f71e:
In the run above, the vector approach sums five rows that are all "similar" and lands about 12 percent away from the truth. On a real account with hundreds of rows the error is arbitrary.

And the vector route is not merely inaccurate. It is unauditable, because there is no query to show an auditor. The SQL tool is a single parameterised statement with a result you can reproduce.
b5e69f9053:
Sometimes the questions are too varied for a fixed set of tools, and teams let the model write SQL. That is a legitimate design when the guard is code. The model proposes a statement, and a validator that you wrote decides whether it runs.

At minimum, the validator must:

  • accept a single read-only SELECT;
  • require a predicate binding the tenant or account to the session's value;
  • reject anything it cannot parse;
  • run on a read-only connection with a statement timeout and a row limit.

Example 02 shows the first two checks on five hostile or careless statements. A production guard parses the SQL (a real parser, not a regular expression) and checks every table in the statement against an allow-list.

Prefer the fixed-tool design when you can enumerate the top ten questions. It has no injection surface, its latency is predictable, and its tests are ordinary unit tests.
292b152e0c: For a Spring team this is a familiar shape. The tool is a service method behind a facade. The session supplies the principal. The model-facing description is generated from the method's contract. The important line is the one that takes the account from the authenticated principal, not from the tool arguments.
bf510b4022: A lexical index maps each term to the list of documents containing it (an inverted index). It ranks documents by how well their terms match the query's. Nearly every engine today uses BM25 as its default ranking function. It is worth deriving, because three of its pieces explain behaviour you will see in production.
e83585f9e2:
Inverse document frequency. A query term that appears in nearly every document says little about which document you want. A term that appears in one says a great deal. The common form is idf(t) = ln(1 + (N − nt + 0.5) / (nt + 0.5)), where N is the number of documents and nt the number containing the term.

In the 77-chunk toy corpus, the code err-5g-4417 appears in two chunks (idf about 3.4) and baseband in one (about 3.95). phone, in four, gets 2.85, and credit, in seven, gets 2.3. In a corpus of millions of chunks the gap widens. That is why an error code is easy for a lexical index: it is the rarest, highest-weighted thing in the query.
e14e710a94:
Term-frequency saturation. A document that mentions a word ten times is more likely to be about that word than one that mentions it twice. But it is not five times more likely. BM25 passes the raw count f through f(k1 + 1) / (f + k1), which rises quickly and flattens toward k1 + 1. With k1 = 1.2, the second occurrence is worth about 1.4 times the first, and the tenth about 2.0 times. With k1 = 0 the count is ignored completely.

This stops a keyword-stuffed chunk from beating a good one. It is also why a chunk that repeats a code in its title and body does not run away with the ranking.
5e63ca04c2:
Length normalisation. A long chunk contains more words, so it matches more query words by chance. BM25 divides by a term that grows with the chunk's length relative to the average. The parameter b controls it: 0 means ignore length, 1 means full normalisation, and 0.75 is the usual default.

This interacts directly with chapter 8. Chunk size changes the average length, and very short chunks (a title and one line) are advantaged. Together:
846be755a5:
BM25 ranks tokens. So what counts as a token is the most consequential setting in the lexical index, and the one most often left at its default.

A standard text analyzer lower-cases, splits on punctuation, and may stem. Applied to ERR-5G-4471 it produces err, 5g and 4471. The query for the code is analysed the same way. So a chunk containing those three tokens in any order matches. So does every chunk that contains err and 5g, which in an error-code catalogue means thousands of them. Only the rare 4471 token rescues the ranking. When the numeric part of a code is common (LU-3 splits into lu and 3), nothing rescues it.

The fix is a tokenizer rule that keeps hyphenated alphanumeric identifiers whole, applied exactly the same way to queries. (You can also index both the whole token and its parts, which costs index size.)

Example 04 measures the damage as the margin: the gap between the score of the right chunk and the runner-up. A thin margin makes a confidence gate (section 14) unreliable. A score that barely separates the right answer from the wrong one cannot be thresholded.
881efe1868:
Both analyzers find the right chunk on this corpus. The point is the mean margin falling from 68 to 53 percent, plus the stray low-scoring matches (the last line) that appear when the code is split. On a catalogue of tens of thousands of codes with shared prefixes, the margin loss turns into wrong top-1 results.

This is a classic exam trap. A vector database "does not find part numbers", and the proposed fix is a bigger embedding model. The real fix is a lexical leg with a sane analyzer.
e950619bf9:
Chapter 8 section 05 gave the schema: a generated tsvector column with a GIN index. The caveat from there stands. ts_rank and ts_rank_cd are not BM25 (no collection-wide idf, a different length treatment), and for an engineering corpus full of codes the differences can matter. Extensions and external engines provide true BM25 (check the docs for the options at your version).

Two practical points belong here.

First, websearch_to_tsquery parses user-style queries safely. That matters, because a raw query string with stray operators raises an error in to_tsquery.

Second, the default english text-search configuration stems and removes stop words. That is right for prose and wrong for codes. Consider a second column with the simple configuration for identifiers, and a rule to extract codes into their own indexed field.

An exact-key table for codes (a plain B-tree lookup on a normalised code) is the cheapest and most precise retriever for a query that is nothing but a code. That is why the router of section 05 sends bare codes to "lexical / key".
8f38c23df1:
A dense retriever maps text to a vector so that texts with similar meaning land near each other. It answers a query by finding the stored vectors nearest to the query's. What "near" means is learned from data. The encoder was trained so that, for example, a question and the passage that answers it end up close together.

That is what lets "how do I get out of my contract early" find a chunk titled "Early termination fee", which shares no content word with the question. For prose in varied vocabulary, nothing lexical matches that.
1ad49df73c:
The same property causes the characteristic failure. An encoder compresses a passage into a fixed number of dimensions. Meaning survives compression. The exact spelling of a rare token mostly does not.

To a subword tokenizer, ERR-5G-4471 and ERR-5G-4474 are nearly the same sequence of pieces, with one different at the end. Nothing in the training objective made the model care which digit that was. In the toy vectors of example 05, the cosine similarity between the two codes is 0.83, and the query for 4471 ranks the 4474 article first. A real model will not be so crude, but the direction is the same. And it gets worse as the catalogue grows, because there are more siblings.

The same blur affects product names that differ by a suffix (a Galaxy S24 case and a Galaxy S24 Ultra case). It affects negations: an encoder may rate "covered" and "not covered" as close. And it affects numbers ("30 days" against "15 days").
0a4cf07264: Read the first block of that output. The paraphrase query ranks the superseded 2022 policy ahead of the current one, because the two chunks are nearly identical text with different numbers. A dense retriever cannot know that one is stale. That is a metadata problem (section 10), not an embedding problem, and no amount of model quality fixes it.
cd783279f1:
Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every stored vector. That is fine for a few thousand chunks and too slow for millions. Approximate indexes trade a little recall for a large speed-up. HNSW builds a layered graph of neighbours. A search starts at the top, hops greedily toward the query, and descends.

Three parameters matter:

  • m, the number of links per node;
  • ef_construction, the candidate list size at build time;
  • ef_search, the candidate list size at query time.

The first two fix the quality of the graph, and raising them costs build time and memory. Raising the third improves recall and costs latency, linearly or worse.

In pgvector the names are m, ef_construction and the session setting hnsw.ef_search. The default value of ef_search, the available alternative index types, and the quantisation options have changed across versions (check the docs for your version).

The architect uses these knobs like any others. Measure recall of the approximate index against exact search on a sample of queries. Then choose the cheapest setting that holds your recall bar at your p95.
ca0cf48bac:
The embedding model is a separate choice from the generation model. Anthropic's documentation has said that it does not offer its own embedding model, and it points to third-party providers for embeddings. This may have changed, so check the docs before writing it into a design.

For the exam, the useful rules are model-independent:

  • The query and the chunks must be embedded with the same model and version (chapter 8 part 6 on re-embedding).
  • The dimension and index type must match.
  • Multilingual corpora need a multilingual model.
  • Domain jargon is where a general model most often underperforms, so test it on your labelled queries rather than on a public leaderboard.

Some embedding models are trained with a query/document distinction. The query is encoded with a different instruction or input type than the passages. Using the wrong one is a silent loss of recall (check your provider's docs).
7ecb859dfd:
Lexical search fails on paraphrase, and dense search fails on exact tokens. So run both and combine.

The combination step is where most hybrid systems go wrong, because the two retrievers speak different units. A BM25 score is unbounded and depends on the query length and the corpus. A cosine similarity lies between −1 and 1 and clusters in a narrow band. Adding them lets whichever distribution has an outlier dominate. So does normalising each to 0–1 and then adding.

Example 06 demonstrates it. One extreme BM25 score squeezes every other BM25 score toward zero under min-max normalisation, and changes the fused order.
7e023b7db2:
Reciprocal rank fusion sidesteps the unit problem by using only the ranks. A document's fused score is the sum over retrievers of 1 / (k + rank). Here k is a smoothing constant: 60 in the original paper and the common default.

A document ranked first by both gets 2/61. A document ranked first by one and absent from the other gets 1/61. A document ranked tenth in both gets 2/70, which beats a document that is first in only one list. That last property is the point: agreement between independent retrievers is strong evidence. It is also the property that bites, as the next paragraphs show.
836c62eb45:
Small k (1 to 10) makes the top ranks dominate. A first place counts far more than a fifth place, so a strong single-retriever hit survives. Large k (several hundred or more) flattens the curve until fusion becomes a vote on membership. k = 60 is the original paper's value and a reasonable start. Weights multiply a retriever's contribution.

Look at the run above:

  • With k = 1, the first place counts so much that kb-esim-s24 scores 1.0 against 0.46 for the runner-up.
  • With k = 1000, the fused scores tie to three decimals, and only the order of ties remains.
  • Weighting the lexical leg 2 to 1 leaves the top three unchanged and swaps the fourth place. The long device-heavy query gives the lexical leg several strong matches on "galaxy" and "s24" (the two case listings).

Weights matter at the margin, which is where a hit at rank 4 or 5 lives. There is no universal weight. If you tune weights, tune them per segment against the labelled set. Hold out queries you did not tune on, and treat the result as provisional until chapter 11's evaluation is run on fresh data.

The segments suggest the structure. Error-code queries benefit from a heavier lexical weight, and paraphrase queries from a heavier dense weight. A router that already knows the segment can set them.
d052c1eb8c:
The segment table above is deliberately uncomfortable. Plain RRF hybrid scores 0.89 recall@5 against BM25's 0.90 on this corpus. On paraphrase it is no better than BM25 (0.85), even though the vector index alone scores 1.00.

The reason is visible in the data. For "can I send my phone back", BM25 returns many chunks about phones and nothing about returns. The vector index ranks the return policy first. Fusion puts the policy sixth, because it is present in only one list. That is how a fusion can lower the best retriever's result: the other retriever returns confident junk.

Three responses exist, and the chapter returns to all of them:

  • weight or route by segment (this section);
  • rerank the fused candidates so a stronger scorer decides (section 12);
  • fix the vocabulary gap at the query (section 11).

Hybrid remains the sound default for mixed workloads, because it protects against the failure of either leg. But the exam answer is rarely "hybrid" alone. When it is, the scenario describes a corpus with both codes and prose.
8cf41fdd79: With the chapter 8 schema, both legs and the fusion run in the database, with the permission and currency filters inside each leg. For a team already operating Postgres, this is the simplest architecture that works. (The statement is shown for structure. It was not executed in this environment, so check it on your version.)
c60723355d:
Ranking answers "which of these candidates is best". Filtering answers "which candidates are allowed to be considered at all". Mixing the two up causes three of the most common production defects in retrieval: forbidden content reaching the prompt, stale content outranking current content, and missing results for small customers.

Chapter 8 part 4 put the metadata into the index (tenant, ACL groups, document type, device, effective date, is_current). This section is about how the query uses it.
b65c9fe2fd:
A filter can be applied in two places. A pre-filter (or filtered search) restricts the candidate set before ranking, so the top k are the best of the allowed chunks. A post-filter ranks the whole index, takes the top candidates, and then drops the ones that fail the filter.

With a lexical index that does a full scan of matching postings, the difference is small. With an approximate vector index it is large. The index returns a fixed number of candidates for the query (ef_search in HNSW), and the WHERE clause is applied to those.

Say the index returns forty candidates. If the filter keeps one chunk in ten, you get about four results. If it keeps one in fifteen, about three. If the question happens to be about something outside the allowed set, none. Then the application reports "no answer" for a question that has one. No error is raised at any point.
a06ee7a2c3:
pgvector's HNSW index applies the filter after the index scan. Versions that support iterative scans can keep scanning until enough rows pass. Partitioning by tenant, or a partial index per large tenant, sidesteps the problem (chapter 8 part 5; check the docs for your version's behaviour and parameter names). Other engines implement filtered search inside the graph traversal.

The architect's test is independent of engine. Take a small tenant, ask a question you know it can answer, and count the results. If the count drops as the filter gets more selective, you have a post-filter.
370533d762:
The rule from chapter 7 applies to retrieval without exception. The caller's groups come from the verified identity. They enter the retrieval query as a filter. No chunk the caller may not read is ever fetched. "Fetch then filter in the application" fails the moment anyone adds a second path: a cache, a reranker log, a debug endpoint.

The second rule: anything that stores retrieval results must key on the permission context. Example 09 shows the sharper failure. A retrieval cache is keyed by query text alone. An engineer asks "serving gateway overload what to do first", and the next customer to ask the same words is served the engineer's cached runbook. The fix is a key that includes the ACL class, the tenant and the index version.

The third rule is a test that cannot be skipped. For every role and every labelled query, assert that every returned chunk is within the role's ACL. Example 09 runs it across 3 roles and 44 queries and finds zero leaks with the filter inside the query.
25cd81af73:
The last two lines of that output are the stale-policy defect. Without a currency filter, the 2022 return policy (fifteen days, a restocking fee) is retrieved next to the 2025 one (thirty days) for the same question. The generator has to guess which is true. In five of the labelled queries a superseded chunk appeared in the top five, and in three it outranked the current version. The dense and lexical scores for two near-identical versions are near-identical.

The cure is metadata. Mark old versions is_current = false at ingestion (chapter 8 part 6), and filter on it by default. Expose "as of" queries (effective date at or before a given date) only where a business need exists, such as disputing a charge under the policy that applied then. For questions that depend on a date, put the date in the filter, not the prompt.
a1707833ae:
Some corpora have explicit links: a promotion-stacking rule that names the promotion it excludes, a runbook that says "see the backhaul congestion runbook", a policy that supersedes another. A question that spans a link ("can the trade-in credit be combined with the loyalty upgrade?") needs both ends. And the second chunk may not resemble the question at all.

The cheapest remedy is one-hop expansion. After retrieval, add the chunks that the top few results reference, with a decayed score so they rank below the seeds that justified them. Chapter 8 stored the links as a refs field, and example 10 uses it.

The measurement is the point. The multi-hop segment's recall@5 rises from 0.88 to 1.00. Meanwhile precision@5 and the context size on the other segments barely move, because few of their top results carry references.
120aabd52b:
Graph-based approaches go further. They extract entities and relations into a knowledge graph, store them in a graph or relational structure, and answer questions by traversing it or by retrieving community summaries. Microsoft's GraphRAG paper of 2024 is the usual reference.

The exam-level judgement is the same as everywhere. Those systems cost ingestion time and operational complexity. Use them when the questions are genuinely about relationships across many documents, and a one-hop expansion or a SQL join measurably fails. In the telecom estate, the relationships often already live in a relational model (customer to plan to feature to promotion). There a join is both simpler and exact.
8c1c643400:
The user's words are not always the best search query. A model can transform the query before it reaches the retrievers. Three transformations are worth separating, because they have different benefits and different risks.

  • Contextualisation turns a follow-up ("and can I combine it with autopay?") into a standalone query that carries what the earlier turns established ("iPhone 15 Pro trade-in credit combined with autopay discount"). Without it, the retriever sees a few words and a pronoun.
  • Vocabulary expansion adds the policy's words to the user's words. "how long do I have to send a phone back" gains "return window", which is how the policy is written. This cures the lexical leg's paraphrase weakness, and the vector leg's occasional drift.
  • Decomposition splits a compound question into sub-queries that are searched separately and merged. It is the bridge toward agentic retrieval (section 13).
f58ad77a13:
In example 11, the first transformation moves the best rank of the relevant chunk from 3 to 1. The second moves it from rank 6 in the hybrid (absent from BM25's top 20) to rank 1 in both. Those are the gains.

The costs come in three parts. First, a model call before any retrieval can start. It sits on the critical path, at 300 to 900 milliseconds in the planning numbers, and it is the largest optional retrieval-side item in example 14. Second, a few hundred tokens. Third, a new failure mode: the rewriter can drop or alter the very tokens the lexical leg needed.

The third case in the example shows it. The scripted model rewrites "customer got ERR-5G-4474 on attach" as "customer attach failure error on registration". That reads fine, and it loses the one token that identifies the answer. The relevant chunk disappears from the top twenty. A code-level guard restores it: check that every identifier in the original appears in the rewrite, and append any that are missing.
3481037981:
Skip the rewrite in four cases:

  • queries that are already standalone and short;
  • bare identifiers, which a rewrite can only damage;
  • latency budgets with no slack (example 14: adding the rewrite pushes p95 from 1.7 seconds to 2.2 seconds, which is inside a 2.5 second budget and over an 1.8 second one);
  • when a cheaper mechanism closes the same gap.

A maintained synonym map ("send back" to "return", "repair" to "warranty") costs nothing at query time and is easy to review. Example 16 uses one and measures it. The caution travels with it. A synonym list written after reading the failures of a test set has been tuned on that set. Its apparent gain must be re-measured on queries it has not seen.

HyDE (embedding a model-written hypothetical answer instead of the question) is a related trick for dense retrieval, for when queries and passages differ in style. It costs a generation call and can hallucinate terms, so apply the same measure-then-keep rule.
dfc6ca70c8:
A first-stage retriever scores the query and each chunk independently. A vector index compares two fixed vectors. BM25 counts matching tokens. Neither reads the query and the passage together. So neither can see that a chunk is about the right product but answers a different question.

A reranker does read them together. A cross-encoder passes the pair through a model and outputs a relevance score. An LLM-based reranker is asked to rate or order the passages. That joint reading is why a reranker is more accurate. It is also why it is expensive: its cost grows linearly with the number of candidates, because each one needs a forward pass with the query.

The standard design is the funnel. A cheap first stage retrieves a generous candidate set for recall. The reranker orders it for precision. Only the top few go to the model.
2936b0478d:
Read the sweep like a procurement decision. On this corpus, reranking the fused top 10 lifts recall@5 from 0.89 to 0.94, and MRR from 0.88 to 0.91. Reranking 77 candidates (the whole corpus, equivalent to ranking everything with the expensive model) adds 107 milliseconds and nothing else.

The candidate depth you need is set by where the relevant chunks sit in the first-stage ranking, and you can measure that. Compute the rank of the first relevant chunk across the labelled set, and take, say, the 95th percentile. If that is 18, a depth of 20 to 30 is enough, and 100 is waste. If it is 90, the fix is probably in the first stage, not in a deeper rerank.

In the companion set, the median first-stage rank of a relevant chunk is 1, the 95th percentile is 6, and the maximum is 10. That is exactly why the sweep above flattens at depth 10: there is nothing beyond rank 10 for a deeper rerank to find.
e19e312bc9:
Three design points matter beyond depth.

First, a reranker has a different failure surface from the retrievers. The stand-in in the companion is a hand-written scorer with a concept feature. Like a real one, it can fix a vocabulary gap that the lexical leg missed (the "send my phone back" query reaches the top five). And like a real one, it can still be wrong about negation and numbers. Evaluate it per segment, like everything else.

Second, hosted rerank APIs exist from several vendors. A Claude model can also serve as an LLM reranker: pass the query and numbered candidates, and ask for a ranking or scores. That costs tokens per candidate (the example's last two columns, with placeholder pricing) and a full model-call latency. So reserve it for low-volume, high-value flows such as agent-assist, and check the docs for hosted options, limits and prices.

Third, a reranker can return a calibrated, or at least monotone, score. That gives you the confidence gate of section 14 almost for free.
998a861e98:
Some questions cannot be answered by a fixed retrieval step, because what to look for next depends on what the first lookup returned. "Can the iPhone 15 Pro trade-in credit be combined with the autopay discount?" needs the trade-in policy. That policy mentions rule PS-12, which also needs to be read. A system that exposes search as a tool lets the model make that second search itself.

The loop is the one from chapter 2. The model proposes a tool call, the harness runs it, and the result goes back. Then the model proposes the next call, or answers. For retrieval, this is the most flexible design, and the most expensive.
a69b1a8bf6:
Compute the economics first. Each step is a model call plus a search, around 1.4 seconds at the median in the planning numbers, and the steps run in sequence. Three steps plus the final answer means four model calls before the first token of the answer. The variance compounds too. Example 14's agent configuration has a p50 of 4.4 seconds and a p95 of 6.9, against 0.9 and 1.7 for the hybrid-plus-rerank pipeline.

Against a 2.5 second first-token SLA, the agent fails by construction, whatever its accuracy. Against an 8 second agent-assist draft SLA it fits, if you cap the steps. So the same question gets a different design depending on who is waiting. That is why the requirements card records both numbers.
f9abb739f3:
Four controls belong on every retrieval loop, and the example has the first three.

  • A step budget (four here) ends the loop and returns what it has. A model that keeps searching is a cost incident.
  • A duplicate-query guard tells the model it already asked that, instead of burning a call.
  • A trace records every query and result id. A wrong answer can then be explained, and an auditor can see which chunks the model saw.
  • the same permission filter runs inside the search tool as everywhere else. The tool takes the caller's identity from the harness, never from the model's arguments.

Add per-request cost and latency caps in the harness. Then decide what the loop returns when a cap triggers. An honest "I could not complete the search" is better than an answer from partial evidence.
72b987df73:
The last block of the output compares the loop with a fixed alternative: hybrid retrieval plus one-hop expansion from section 10. The fixed version finds both required chunks in one retrieval and one model call, because the link is explicit in the data.

The decision rule that follows comes from the pattern ladder:

  • Where the chain of lookups is enumerable and explicit (references, parent-child, supersession), use a fixed pipeline with expansion.
  • Where it is open-ended (the next question depends on a number the first result contained, or on which of several sources has the answer), use the loop, bounded.
  • Where it is structured (customer to plan to feature to price), write the join and expose it as a tool.

In a telecom support assistant, the loop typically handles a few percent of traffic: the rare questions that fall off the fixed paths. The router sends only those to it.
f8e54a9d71:
A related technique reduces what the model sees up front. Instead of returning ten full chunks, the search tool returns ids, titles and a short snippet. A second tool (read_chunk(id)) returns the full text of the ones the model chooses. That is the retrieval analogue of progressive tool discovery (chapter 6): smaller initial context, more calls.

It pays when chunks are large and most of them are irrelevant. It costs a round trip per read, so the same arithmetic applies. For a bounded, latency-sensitive path, prefer the funnel: rerank, then pass the top few full chunks.
3f2b27623a:
Retrieval always returns something. A vector index returns the nearest neighbours of any query, including "what is the weather in Dallas". A BM25 query with one stray matching word returns a chunk. Hand those to the generator, and it will try to answer from them or from its own memory. That is the standard route to a confident hallucination.

The remedy is a gate between retrieval and generation. It decides whether the evidence is sufficient. If not, it sends the conversation down a different path: say that the information was not found, ask a clarifying question, or hand off to a person.
14b69e51ef:
A gate needs a score and a threshold. Raw BM25 scores are not comparable across queries, because they depend on the query length and the terms' idf. Cosine similarities cluster so tightly that a fixed cut-off is fragile.

The most useful signal is a reranker's top score, because the reranker is trained to estimate the relevance of this passage to this query. The second most useful is the margin between the first and second results (which is why the analyzer matters, section 07). Example 17 sweeps the threshold on the stand-in reranker's top score over 40 answerable and 16 unanswerable queries, and prints the trade-off.
e572b6315f:
Two cautions.

The threshold is specific to the scorer, the corpus and the embedding model. Recalibrate when any of them changes. Recalibrate per segment too, if the scores differ (code lookups score differently from policy questions).

And 16 unanswerable queries are too few to set a production threshold. The labelled set should include a real share of the questions your users ask that the corpus cannot answer. You will find those in the logs (chapter 10).
babd712784:
The last retrieval decision is how many chunks, in what order, with what labels. More context is not free (chapter 5). Every chunk adds input tokens, and long contexts are used unevenly. Studies of long-context models (Liu et al., 2023, "Lost in the Middle") found that evidence placed in the middle of a long prompt is used less reliably than evidence at the start or end. Model generations differ, so test your configuration.

Practical rules that hold up:

  • Pass the top few chunks after reranking, not the top fifty.
  • Put the strongest first.
  • Label each chunk with its id and source, so the model can cite it and a person can check it.
  • Include the section path and effective date.
  • Pass neighbouring chunks when a result's meaning depends on its neighbours (a table row, a numbered step), expanding by doc_id and ordinal from chapter 8.
  • Keep retrieved text in a clearly delimited block, treated as data, so instructions inside a document are not obeyed (chapter 13).

The Claude API has features for supplying documents or search results with citation support (check the docs for the current names and constraints). With them, answers can point back to the chunk that supports each claim. That is also the cheapest audit trail you will build.
739bb88743:
A latency SLA is a statement about a percentile of the end-to-end time a user waits. A retrieval pipeline is a chain of stages, each with its own distribution. Two facts from probability govern every budget you will write. Both are routinely mishandled, on the exam and in design reviews.

First, the p95 of a sum is not the sum of the p95s. Take five stages that each take 50 milliseconds at the median and 100 at p95. The sum of medians is 250 and the sum of p95s is 500. But the p95 of the total is about 370 in simulation (example 15), because it is unlikely that all five are slow at once.

Second, the p95 of a maximum is larger than any component's p95. When dense and lexical search run in parallel, the pair takes as long as the slower one. The chance that at least one of two is slow is about double. In example 15, a dense branch with p95 70 milliseconds and a lexical branch with p95 65 give a pair p95 of 83. Parallelism helps the median a lot and the tail a little.
98e087c8e4:
The practical method has five steps.

  1. Set the end-to-end figure by who is waiting. A customer in chat feels time to first token (2.5 seconds p95 in our card). An agent waiting for an assist draft tolerates longer (8 seconds). A nightly batch has no wait at all (chapter 1 section 14).
  2. List the stages, fixed and optional, with a p50 and a p95 from your traces.
  3. Simulate the whole pipeline with those distributions, treating parallel groups as maxima.
  4. Compare the simulated p95 and p99 with the SLA, and keep headroom, because the planning numbers are optimistic about the tail.
  5. Rank the stages by contribution, and cut from the top of the optional list.
34322e965d:
Three readings.

Every configuration except the agent meets 2,500 milliseconds with room to spare. So the SLA alone does not forbid rewriting or reranking. The per-segment accuracy gate decides whether you need them.

Run the same code with --sla 1800, and configuration D (with the rewrite call) violates it while the others still pass. That is exactly when you must pick between a rewrite stage and a tighter customer promise.

And the contribution table shows where the budget goes. Generation is more than half the sum of p95s, and it cannot be traded. The rewrite is nearly a third. The dense search, which engineers worry about, is 4 percent. Optimise in that order, not in the order of what is easy to tune.
4821710510:
Chapter 11 is the full treatment of evaluation: metric families, datasets, graders, statistics. Retrieval is the most measurable part of an LLM system, because scoring it needs no model call. Given a query and the set of chunk ids a person marked relevant, any retriever's output can be scored by arithmetic, in milliseconds. You can do it on every change to the analyzer, the chunker, the embedding model, the filters or the fusion weights.

That makes retrieval metrics the right thing to put in the CI pipeline. The end-to-end answer evaluation of chapter 11 is the slower, more expensive layer above.
77914a5bbb:
Build it from real traffic, by segment:

  • Sample queries from logs, or from the support tickets and chat transcripts that the assistant will replace.
  • Cluster or tag them into the segments of the requirements card.
  • Have a subject-matter expert mark the chunk ids that answer each one, including all chunks of a multi-part answer.
  • Add the unanswerable queries users actually ask.
  • Add the hard negatives you know about (near-duplicate codes, superseded versions, the S24 and the S24 Ultra).
  • Keep a part of it as a hold-out that nobody tunes on.

The size follows from the bar and the arithmetic of chapter 1 example 13. To claim a 95 percent hit rate with 95 percent confidence, you need 59 queries in the segment with no failures, or 93 with one failure. The companion set has 4 to 13 queries per segment. That is enough to demonstrate the machinery and far too small to launch on. The Wilson intervals printed by example 07 (0.60 to 0.98 for 9 of 10) say so plainly.
5ba69cec7b:
With quality measured per segment and latency modelled per configuration, the choice is a table. Example 16 combines them. It shows seven configurations, their overall recall@5 and MRR, the p95 from the budget model, and the segments that fall below their bars.

A configuration is dominated if another is at least as accurate and at least as fast. Drop those. Among the rest, take the cheapest one that meets every bar and the SLA. If none does, the table shows which segment fails. That is the next piece of work, not a reason to buy a bigger component.
b3e2804e3d:
Notice what the table does not say. It does not say hybrid beats BM25 here (0.89 against 0.90, and hybrid is dominated by BM25 on this set). This toy corpus has paraphrase queries that are easy for the lexical leg, and many codes, so plain fusion adds little.

What it does say is that the reranker and the vocabulary fix are where the gains are. And the synonym list was written after reading these failures, so its 0.99 is an upper estimate until held-out queries confirm it.

The right way to read a result like this in an ADR is to write the conclusion that survives the caveats: start with hybrid plus a shallow rerank, add vocabulary expansion for the paraphrase segment, re-measure on held-out queries, and revisit when the corpus doubles.
15f54ab67d:
A retrieval configuration that passed its gate in staging can degrade in production for reasons that have nothing to do with the model. Documents change. An ingestion job silently fails. An embedding model is upgraded for new chunks only. The query mix shifts after a marketing campaign.

Chapter 10 is the full observability chapter. This section lists what retrieval must emit and how to read it.
34e11557b6:
From those, five dashboards earn their place:

  • recall proxy by segment (outcome signals joined to the route);
  • empty-result and abstain rate (a sudden rise means an ingestion failure or a filter bug, and a sudden fall may mean the gate was loosened);
  • p50/p95/p99 per stage (the budget of section 15, measured);
  • degraded-mode rate (how often a branch timed out);
  • index freshness (age of the newest chunk per source, against the 15-minute promise).

Alerts should fire on changes in these, not on their absolute value.
7f328bc663:
Three caches are common, and each has a rule.

A query-embedding cache is safe and useful when users repeat questions. It is keyed by the normalised query and the embedding model version.

A retrieval-result cache must be keyed by query, ACL class, tenant, index version and filter set (example 09 shows the leak when it is not). It must be invalidated or expire when the underlying documents change, with the TTL no longer than the freshness promise.

A semantic cache returns a stored answer for a similar-enough question, and it is the riskiest. "Similar" includes "cancel my line" and "cancel my neighbour's line". Use it only for public, non-personal content, with a high similarity bar and an expiry. Never use it where the answer depends on the account.
6c77d8b66c:
When a user reports a wrong answer, resist the urge to change the prompt. Replay the logged request and ask four questions in order:

  1. Was the right chunk in the first-stage candidate set (recall@50)? If not, the failure is upstream of ranking: the analyzer, the chunking, the embedding, a filter, a stale index, or the query itself (rewrite).
  2. Was it in the candidates but not in the final top five? Then the failure is ranking: fusion weights, the reranker, the depth.
  3. Was it in the final context, but the answer wrong? That is generation or context assembly: position, instructions, conflicting chunks, the model.
  4. Was the right answer correct but late, or missing under load? That is the budget, a degraded branch or a timeout.

The figure turns the questions into a flow, and the table maps each failure to its usual cause and first fix.
cae3f2adfb:
For a Spring team, the retrieval layer is a service that fans out to two repositories. It applies a deadline to each, merges their results, and reports how complete they are. The structure is familiar from scatter-gather integrations. So are the places where it goes wrong: a thread pool shared with unrelated work, a timeout that abandons the response but not the work, and a failure of one branch that fails the whole request.

The class below is plain JDK, so it compiles and runs without Spring. In a service, the two suppliers are injected beans (a JdbcTemplate-backed lexical repository and an embedding-plus-ANN repository), and the executor is a bounded pool you own. The companion's run_all.sh compiles and runs it.
5fe7c86c36:
Three details deserve attention.

First, completeOnTimeout stops the caller waiting. It does not cancel the abandoned query, which keeps a connection and a thread busy until it finishes. Give the underlying clients their own timeouts and cancellation. Wrap them in a circuit breaker, so a failing embedding service stops taking traffic quickly. Resilience4j is the usual choice in Spring (check the docs for the annotation names and configuration of your version).

Second, the unavailable outcome is part of the contract. When both branches fail or time out, the caller must not let the model answer from its own memory. The answer policy in example 18 returns a "cannot look that up right now" message, and a person follows up.

Third, cache annotations are a trap here. Spring's @Cacheable with a default key of the method arguments would key on the query and principal object identity at best, and on the query alone at worst. Build the key explicitly from query, tenant, ACL class and index version. That is the Java equivalent of the fixed cache in example 09.
fb161bb380: Four systems cover most enterprise retrieval work. The configurations below are starting points, chosen by the rules of this chapter. Each must still pass its own segment gate. Latency figures are SLA targets, not measurements.
e0f5964726: An ADR for a retrieval design records four things: the decision, the evidence, the alternatives rejected, and the conditions under which it should be revisited. The numbers below are the illustrative figures from the companion run. Yours will differ.
03e854bf25: CCAR-P gives a data source, a query pattern and a number, then offers four designs. Work each scenario before reading the reasoning. The best answer matches the retriever to the data, justifies any extra stage with a measured gain, and fits the stated budget.
9adcda6def:
Exact identifiers are rare tokens. Embeddings compress them and blur siblings, and a larger model reduces that but does not remove it. A lexical leg ranks the exact token highest. A key lookup is cheaper still for a query that is only a code.

A is expensive and treats the symptom. C reorders candidates, but it cannot rescue a right answer that is not among them, and it costs a model call per query. D raises recall of the candidate set at the cost of precision and latency, and the neighbour code is still ranked above the right code. Measure the code segment on its own bar.
e096e1bc18:
The data is structured, and the question is an aggregate on a key. A typed tool returns the exact answer, reproducibly. The session-bound account closes the cross-tenant risk.

A, C and D keep the model doing arithmetic over whichever rows retrieval happened to return. Retrieval by similarity cannot implement a WHERE clause or a SUM. And the index is a snapshot.
85f6bf15fa:
Add the p95s conservatively: auth 0.1 + hybrid 0.15 + rerank 0.25 + generation 1.2 = 1.7 s, which fits 2.0. Adding the rewrite makes 2.5 s, and an agent step makes 3.2 s or more. So A, and the rewrite in C, break the SLA. Simulate to confirm, since sums of p95s overstate.

The synonym map closes a vocabulary gap at zero query-time cost. The agent path for the small multi-rule segment is justified by its share, and by a different promise. D does not address the measured gap, and a larger model may add latency.
8400d6ae8a:
The symptom is fewer results as the filter gets more selective, with no error. That is the post-filter signature. Filter-then-rank, or partitioning, makes the top k come from the allowed set.

C is a data leak. A and D do not touch the cause. Test with a small tenant and a question it should answer, and count the results as the filter tightens.
d3732befa9:
The requirement is per segment, so the average is irrelevant to whether this segment passes. The diagnosis questions follow the triage flow: was the right chunk in the candidates, and where was it ranked?

A ignores the requirement. C spends latency everywhere to fix one segment. D changes the requirement to fit the system. That is a decision for the requirement owner, not a way to pass an evaluation.

Note too that the segments at 0.92 fail against a 0.95 bar. Say so.
bb64c4805d:
The link is explicit. So a deterministic expansion finds the second chunk in the same retrieval and the same model call (example 10 raises that segment from 0.88 to 1.00 recall@5).

An agent for every question multiplies model calls and tail latency (example 14: p95 6.9 s against 1.7 s). C inflates every prompt and blurs retrieval. D adds noise and tokens, and it does not guarantee the linked chunk is in the 50.
7c5318e853:
The two versions are nearly identical text, so no similarity score can separate them. The difference is metadata.

A depends on the model noticing a date it may not see. C loses the history needed for disputes. D cannot work, because the scorer has no signal for staleness.
a2154a5ec1:
Step 1, the card. Section 04's JSON: five segments with bars, chat first-token p95 of 2.5 s, 15-minute freshness, permissions in the query, an abstain path.

Step 2, route by shape. Account facts (16 percent of traffic) go to the usage and billing tools. The remaining 84 percent is document retrieval. Example 01's router gets 24 of 24 on its labelled set. That is too easy to trust, so collect 200 real requests before relying on it.

Step 3, baseline. Run the simplest candidates over the labelled set (example 07). BM25 passes error codes (1.00) and fails paraphrase (0.85). Vector passes paraphrase (1.00) and fails error codes (0.70) and mixed (0.88). Neither is shippable alone, which matches the data shapes.
a27af12f2f:
Step 4, hybrid plus rerank. Plain RRF fails error codes at 0.90 and paraphrase at 0.85, because a junk-heavy lexical list drags the dense leg's good answer down. Adding a rerank of the fused top 50 raises code to 1.00, paraphrase to 0.92 and mixed to 1.00. The remaining failure is the filtered segment at 0.80: "how long do I have to send a phone back" has no word in common with the return policy.

Step 5, vocabulary. A synonym map is free at query time. The rewrite call would cost about 0.6 s of p95. With the map, every segment clears its bar on this set (example 16). The pick is the 20-candidate rerank, because the relevant chunks all sit within the first ten (p95 rank 6).

Step 6, budget. Simulated p95 is 1.66 s against 2.5 s. The headroom of 0.84 s also pays for the gate.

Step 7, gate. Set the threshold at 0.35 on the reranker score. On this probe set that gives 2 percent false abstain and 12 percent false answer. The output gate and citations catch the remaining false answers (chapter 13).
eaff5c0f57:
Step 8, the launch decision. The numbers say the design is sound. They do not say it is ready. The segments hold 4 to 13 queries each. The synonym list and weights were tuned on the same set. The gate's unanswerable sample is 16.

So the launch plan is shadow mode (chapter 1 section 17) with a 30 percent hold-out, a target of at least 59 queries per segment, and the per-segment table in the dashboard from day one. That is the CCAR-P pattern. The design is chosen by measurement, and the confidence in the measurement is itself measured.
510f823b6b:
A shopper asks: "Does the rugged case fit my Galaxy S24 Ultra, and can I send it back if it doesn't?" Three different data shapes sit inside one sentence.

  • Compatibility is a relation (accessory to device) that lives in the catalogue database. The query is a join. An embedding search would happily return the S24 case, because the titles differ by one word (the corpus has both, cat-case-s24 and cat-case-s24u).
  • The return policy is versioned prose: hybrid with is_current.
  • Order and stock status, if asked, are API calls.

The router (or the model, calling tools) issues the compatibility lookup and the policy search in parallel. Their latencies overlap, so the retrieval p95 is the slower of the two, not the sum. The generation call follows.
12a2a6831c:
The design costs three small calls, two of them parallel, and one model call to compose the answer.
